strings.name: Katalin Karikó
strings.summary: Karikó pursued the therapeutic potential of mRNA despite funding and career setbacks. With Drew Weissman and colleagues, she found that nucleoside modification could reduce inflammation and improve protein production. This foundational work helped enable COVID-19 mRNA vaccines and brought them the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Her career illustrates sustained basic research and cross-institutional collaboration.
strings.coverageNote: Sources checked through 13 November 2026. Selected milestones do not constitute an exhaustive record of all news or controversies.
strings.influence.rationale: Advanced nucleoside-modified mRNA research, providing key technical foundations for new vaccines and other medical applications.
strings.facts.fact-01.label: Birthplace
strings.facts.fact-02.label: Education
strings.facts.fact-02.value: PhD in biochemistry, University of Szeged (1982)
strings.highlights.highlight-01.title: Foundational modified-mRNA advances
strings.highlights.highlight-01.text: With Weissman and colleagues, developed important methods to reduce RNA immune stimulation and improve protein expression.
strings.highlights.highlight-02.title: From research to applications
strings.highlights.highlight-02.text: Worked on RNA technologies in academia and at BioNTech; vaccines also depended on other teams’ delivery, trials and manufacturing.
strings.timeline.event-01.title: Discussed science with students
strings.timeline.event-01.text: Spoke to secondary school students in Szeged about her career and mRNA research.
strings.timeline.event-02.title: Shared the Nobel Prize
strings.timeline.event-02.text: Awarded with Weissman for nucleoside-modification discoveries enabling effective COVID-19 mRNA vaccines.
strings.timeline.event-03.title: Joined BioNTech
strings.timeline.event-03.text: Brought long-standing RNA expertise into company research and later served as senior vice president.
strings.timeline.event-04.title: Published pivotal RNA research
strings.timeline.event-04.text: With Weissman and colleagues, showed that nucleoside modification reduced unwanted immune responses.
strings.timeline.event-05.title: Joined the University of Pennsylvania
strings.timeline.event-05.text: Continued exploring mRNA therapies and developed a long collaboration with Weissman.
strings.timeline.event-06.title: Moved to the United States
strings.timeline.event-06.text: Left Hungary and initially pursued postdoctoral research at Temple University.
strings.timeline.event-07.title: Completed her doctorate in Szeged
strings.timeline.event-07.text: Completed biochemistry training, with early research involving RNA.
strings.timeline.event-08.title: Born in Hungary
strings.timeline.event-08.text: Born in Szolnok and grew up in Kisújszállás.
